facts.raw_span: A 64-year-old white man was admitted in March 2016 with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia
he had been on therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal “pre-shimmering”
two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, first noted in August 2015
biopsies at that time showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy
he was hemodynamically stable but had a hemoglobin level of 4.4 mmol/L
he reported no weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms
α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels within normal ranges
abdominal ultrasound revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding
contrast-enhanced CT confirmed active bleeding from one of the two hypervascular lesions in segment IV
after angiographic embolization and conservative management, bleeding resolved
follow-up CT showed persistent hypervascular lesions without typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma
MRI demonstrated hypervascular lesions with central necrosis
A 64-year-old white man was admitted in March 2016 with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia
he had been on therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal “pre-shimmering”
two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, first noted in August 2015
biopsies at that time showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy
he was hemodynamically stable but had a hemoglobin level of 4.4 mmol/L
he reported no weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms
α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels within normal ranges
abdominal ultrasound revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding
contrast-enhanced CT confirmed active bleeding from one of the two hypervascular lesions in segment IV
after angiographic embolization and conservative management, bleeding resolved
follow-up CT showed persistent hypervascular lesions without typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma
MRI demonstrated hypervascular lesions with central necrosis

concepts.why: The patient has a history of two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, which were biopsied and shown to be histologically proven adenoma without malignancy, and the current presentation with active bleeding from one of these lesions is consistent with a complication of hepatic adenoma.

Although the initial biopsies showed no malignancy, the patient's presentation with active bleeding and the presence of hypervascular lesions with central necrosis on MRI raise the suspicion for an atypical hepatocellular carcinoma, which is a possible diagnosis that needs to be ruled out with further evaluation.

The patient's presentation with subcapsular hepatic bleeding and active bleeding from a hypervascular lesion could also be consistent with a hemorrhagic liver cyst, although this diagnosis is less likely given the history of biopsied adenomas.
The patient's hypervascular lesions with central necrosis on MRI could also be consistent with focal nodular hyperplasia, a benign liver lesion that can present with similar imaging characteristics.

rationales.F03: Hypervascular liver lesions are more common in hepatic adenoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.
rationales.F04: Biopsy-proven adenoma without malignancy strongly supports hepatic adenoma and rules out hepatocellular carcinoma.
rationales.F08: Subcapsular hepatic bleeding is more typical of hemorrhagic liver cyst.
rationales.F09: Active bleeding from a hypervascular lesion is more typical of hepatic adenoma or hepatocellular carcinoma.
